items.title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Clinical and Genomic Prognostic Factors for Progression-Free Survival in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Phase III MONALEESA Trials
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy have become widely adopted as a first-line treatment approach for hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC). Through a collaboration between Novartis and the US Food and Drug Administration, we integrated multimodal data from phase III MONALEESA trials to identify novel prognostic factors for HR+/HER2- ABC. Experimental Design: Baseline clinical and genomics data were collected from patients in the MONALEESA-2, -3, and -7 trials. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma samples and gene expression in archival tumor biopsies were analyzed. Machine learning models were trained (n = 1,355) on progression-free survival (PFS) using multimodal features via fusion models. In a test set (n = 382), prognostic performances were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull models. Results: The late fusion model achieved a prognostic performance (C-index: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.641-0.799) slightly outperforming early fusion (C-index: 0.718, 95% CI: 0.631-0.791) and single-modality models. Model-based risk stratification identified distinct low- and high-risk groups (PFS HR, 0.28; 95% CI: 0.20-0.38). Among the top 40 features for progression risk (18 clinical, 20 gene expression, and 2 ctDNA), these were associated with higher risk: liver involvement, higher histological grades, early relapse; lower STC2 and RBBP8 expressions and higher FBX05 expression; and higher tumor mutational burden and ctDNA purity. Conclusions: Integrating clinical and genomic modalities improved progression risk prediction compared with single-modality models, while highlighting salient features that inform the underlying biology and support hypothesis generation.

items.title: UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking
items.abstract_or_text: Medical Concept Recognition is the task of extracting and grounding spans in medical text to entries in a standard ontology. Current methods are generally developed towards a single ontology and source text type (clinical notes, drug labels, etc.) The central challenge is therefore to build methods that adapt to any target ontology without requiring ontology-specific retraining. More recent approaches like REAL and AutoPCR make direct use of Large Language Models and can theoretically adapt to any ontology choice but suffer from a lack of generalization. We propose UMCR, a pipeline that allows extraction and linking to any target ontology using any source text variety, utilizing direct guideline integration and an agentic linking module. We evaluate our method on the recent MedPath benchmark, covering a wide variety of medical text types and vocabularies, and show that our method achieves strong performance across these tasks. This ability unlocks interoperability in the healthcare domain, allowing for extraction and alignment between different medical standards. Our method also reduces dependence on parametric LLM memory, thanks to improved interaction with the target ontology compared to other proposed approaches.

items.title: Affinity maturation of a single-domain antibody via rational mutagenesis informed by artificial intelligence
items.abstract_or_text: Antibodies can originate from various sources such as animal immunizations, patient material, DNA/RNA libraries and (AI-based) de novo design. Pre-made (e.g. synthetic) DNA libraries have substantial advantages over traditional immunization campaigns in terms of speed, cost, animal welfare, amount of required antigen and the possibility to select against otherwise problematic (e.g. toxic, unstable or expensive) antigens. The main downside is that selections from these non-immune libraries often result in binders with relatively low affinity due to the absence of in vivo affinity maturation. Now that in silico structure prediction tools are coming of age, the resulting models could conceivably be used to rationally design mutations, e.g. to enhance binding affinity. Here we used a synthetic single-domain antibody (sdAb) library to select new binders against interleukin-12 (IL-12). One of the selected candidates, 2F3, was predicted to bind to the p40 subunit of IL-12 in a manner that would compete with binding of the receptor protein IL-12R{beta}1. Intriguingly, this epitope is also targeted by the clinically approved antibodies Briakinumab and Ustekinumab, which are used to treat a variety of inflammation disorders. The predicted structure of the IL-12/sdAb complex was used to rationally design eleven point mutations, of which three showed to enhance the binding affinity. By combining these mutations, we could enhance the affinity by eightfold compared to the original lead clone. This shows that correctly (AI-)predicted protein structural models can be used for rational mutagenesis to enhance binding affinity to relevant drug targets.

items.title: Human-Guided Agentic AI for End-to-End EHR Research: Sequential Antibody-Drug Conjugate Pathways in Breast Cancer
items.abstract_or_text: PURPOSE: To demonstrate an end-to-end research workflow combining a large electronic health record (EHR) resource and a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system governed by Human-Guided Orchestration (HGO), using sequential sacituzumab govitecan (SG) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) orders in breast cancer as the clinical use case. METHODS: A June 2026 EHR release contained 4.95 million patients, including 156,051 with breast cancer codes. Muse Spark supported cohort construction, executable statistical analysis, data-quality checks, literature retrieval, and reporting executed through Symbiotic Agent Teaming (SAT) under investigator direction. The main clinical measure was the second-drug record span, from first to last order. Analyses were descriptive and unadjusted; orders did not confirm administration or progression. RESULTS: The workflow identified 106 patients: 73 had T-DXd ordered first and 33 had SG ordered first. Median second-drug spans were 63 days (interquartile range [IQR], 29-116) for SG after T-DXd and 49 days (IQR, 21-126) for T-DXd after SG; the median difference was -14 days (95% bootstrap CI, -41 to 21; distributional P = 0.42). Reported outputs additionally included cohort definitions, aggregate analyses, evidence context, figures, and a preliminary draft manuscript. CONCLUSION: This study provides a concrete model for integrating large EHR resources, agentic AI, and human expertise across the research cycle. The ADC use case illustrates how computational execution and Expert-in-the-Loop (EITL) adjudication can produce interpretable research outputs and refine their scientific meaning, providing a foundation for extending and evaluating this approach across clinical questions.

items.title: Beyond ICD Codes: Semantic IDs for Generative Medical Coding
items.abstract_or_text: Generative approaches to automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding use large language models (LLMs) to predict ICD codes from clinical documents. However, original ICD code strings are not ideal generation targets because the ICD hierarchy does not always reflect clinical relationships, and LLMs struggle to interpret and generate these codes. We introduce SemICD, a framework that trains LLMs to generate Semantic IDs (SIDs) instead. SemICD constructs SIDs by hierarchically clustering embeddings of textual code profiles, allowing semantically related codes to share prefixes while each complete SID uniquely identifies one ICD code. To align the SID tokens with clinical semantics, we employ two auxiliary tasks for bidirectional generation between textual code profiles and SIDs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLMs show that SemICD outperforms direct code generation, improving Micro-F1 by 1.34-8.00 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/SemICD.

items.title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
items.abstract_or_text: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.

items.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

items.title: PlantGeneAnn: a high-accuracy ab initio plant gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model
items.abstract_or_text: Structural annotation remains a bottleneck for translating the growing catalog of high-quality plant genomes into biological insights, as current pipelines rely on RNA-seq and homologous protein evidence that are often unavailable for non-model species. Existing ab initio tools are constrained by model scale and perform poorly in complex plant genomic regions. We present PlantGeneAnn, a plant-optimized ab initio gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model. It combines a Mamba-MoE DNA encoder with a U-Net-style embedding decoder and a semi-Markov decoding pipeline. Trained on 40 angiosperm species, PlantGeneAnn establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) across a stringent 20-species benchmark, significantly outperforming Helixer, Tiberius, and ANNEVO at exon-, intron-, and locus-levels, with mean F1 scores of 0.856, 0.880, and 0.707, respectively. It also enables efficient customized fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tuning increased the locus-level F1 of the out-of-distribution bryophyte Physcomitrium patens from 0.581 to 0.736, with performance plateauing at 40% of the fine-tuning data. Notably, PlantGeneAnn requires substantially lower peak memory usage than other baseline tools, allowing annotation of large plant genomes on standard personal workstations. PlantGeneAnn thus provides accurate, hardware-friendly ab initio annotation for diverse plant genomes, particularly newly assembled genomes, population-scale projects, and non-model plants.

items.title: Deep Learning and Radiomics Models for Predicting 90-Day Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Background Accurate prediction of 90-day outcomes following ischemic stroke is crucial for optimizing clinical strategies. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze studies using deep learning (DL) and hand-crafted radiomics (HCR) models for predicting 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes after ischemic stroke. Methods We followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library) were searched comprehensively for studies published up to September 2025. Inclusion criteria encompassed original research focusing on ischemic stroke patients with mRS at 90 days as the primary outcome and predictive models utilizing imaging biomarkers from CT or MRI. Quality assessment of the included studies was conducted using the PROBAST and and METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) tools. Results Seventeen studies were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Models demonstrated good prognostic performance for 90-day outcomes, with pooled AUCs of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.80-0.86) for internal and 0.74 (95% CI: 0.67-0.89) for external validation sets, with no significant difference (p=0.42). Deep learning and hand-crafted radiomics models showed comparable diagnostic accuracy in the primary analysis (p=0.667); a difference in sensitivity favouring hand-crafted radiomics emerged only in a post-hoc analysis after exclusion of one outlier study. Models incorporating clinical variables significantly outperformed imaging-only models (p<0.01). CT- and MRI-based models showed similar performance. Treatment-specific analyses revealed higher sensitivity for IVT-based models and higher specificity for combined MT+IVT models. Conclusions DL and HCR models demonstrate robust potential for predicting 90-day outcomes in ischemic stroke. Future research should focus on standardizing model evaluation metrics and incorporating explainable AI techniques to improve clinical applicability.

items.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
items.abstract_or_text: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main{GitHub}

items.title: PROTEAN: Beyond De Novo Generation - Can LLM Agents Perform Text-Guided Protein Structure Editing?
items.abstract_or_text: Generative AI has achieved remarkable success in de novo protein design, yet protein engineering typically begins with existing, characterized proteins. The primary demand is targeted local editing, e.g., engineering a specific region to optimize affinity, alter immunogenicity, or improve stability, while strictly preserving core catalytic motifs and overall scaffold integrity. However, no standardized framework currently exists for carrying out and evaluating such edits. In current generative-design workflows, researchers often need to manually specify complex low-level parameters and rely on repetitive, trial-and-error sampling and evaluation across generative backends to search for viable conformations. While large language models (LLMs) offer an intuitive interface to express these goals using natural language, prevailing structure-generation models cannot directly interpret high-level human instructions. To bridge this gap, we introduce PROTEAN, a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing. PROTEAN comprises 380 sub-tasks spanning six intervention families and evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which an LLM translates natural-language goals into backend-specific geometric constraints and a generative model remodels the protein backbone. A two-tier evaluation separates geometric compliance, including target attainment and off-target scope fidelity, from biophysical realizability assessed by inverse folding and refolding consistency. Across five frontier LLMs paired with three backends, strict end-to-end biophysical success starts at just 7.0%. Ablation studies show that LLM constraint compilation is already highly accurate, whereas the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage and refolding failure. PROTEAN provides an open testbed for developing autonomous, multi-backend macromolecular design agents.

items.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
items.abstract_or_text: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

items.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning in Oncology
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning has enabled substantial advances in oncology, including cancer detection and diagnosis, medical image analysis, tumor characterization, treatment planning, response assessment, and outcome prediction. However, conventional data-driven models often require large annotated datasets, exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings, and lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating the physical, physiological, and biological principles underlying cancer development and treatment. Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) integrates governing physical laws, mechanistic models, physiological constraints, and domain knowledge into deep learning frameworks, providing a principled approach for learning from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous oncological data. This review presents a task-oriented synthesis of PIDL methods across oncology, encompassing neural networks, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, convolutional and vision architectures, neural operators, generative models, and hybrid physics-data-driven frameworks. Their applications are examined across cancer detection and diagnosis, image reconstruction and analysis, tumor characterization, quantitative imaging, tumor progression, treatment response, radiation therapy, treatment planning, and multimodal clinical modeling. Based on the synthesized methodological and application-level evidence, we develop task-optimized PIDL workflows that align the clinical task with appropriate data representations, physical constraints, model architectures, and validation strategies. We further analyze key challenges, including physical-model fidelity, computational scalability, uncertainty quantification, domain generalization, standardized benchmarking, and clinical validation.

items.title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

items.title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
items.abstract_or_text: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.

items.title: Joint Variable Selection for Omic Biomarkers in Time-to-Event Data
items.abstract_or_text: The incidence of the vast majority of neurodegenerative, cancer, and metabolic diseases generally increases exponentially with age. In large-scale biobanks, linking time-to-diagnosis information in electronic health records to multiple genomic (``multiomics'') measures has the potential to reveal the genes and biological pathways involved in the disease onset and progression. To date, association testing has commonly been conducted by testing one variable at a time using semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) models, which ignores correlation structure and increases the risk of false discoveries. To address these issues, we introduce a novel fully parametric Bayesian computational method, vampW, based on the Vector Approximate Message Passing framework applied to a Weibull model. vampW jointly models correlated features, while providing an interpretable hazard structure, producing a continuous survival curve, and incorporating prior knowledge. In an extensive simulation study, we demonstrate that joint modeling of omics data and time-to-event outcomes with vampW, substantially reduces false discoveries in comparison to marginal testing and other forms of joint CoxPH models. In 53,018 individuals from the UK Biobank, vampW identifies 219 protein associations with 24 disease outcomes, most of which are not among the top marginal discoveries. We further correct protein levels for exponential age effects, identifying 1,308 associations and highlighting the sensitivity of the analysis to age-correction methodology. Our findings replicate in independent cohorts using different measurement technologies, within data from Iceland and a novel Generation Scotland proteomics dataset. vampW also achieves significant improvement in the prediction of disease onset times: across 14 outcomes, it reduces the root mean squared error by over 30% and 26%, when compared to CoxPH variants and the deep learning approach DeepSurv, respectively, while maintaining predictive utility in minority populations. In summary, vampW offers accurate and interpretable variable selection and out-of-sample prediction within a single computational framework, making it a powerful tool for dissecting the genomic architecture of common complex disease onset.

items.title: Feasibility and Measurement Properties of a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient Laboratory for Clinical Reasoning Training in Physical Therapy Students: Single-Arm Pilot Study
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Large language models (LLMs) configured as virtual patients may expand structured practice of clinical reasoning in health professions education. Before testing effectiveness, it must be established whether students engage with them and whether the resulting scores are complete, reliable, and related to performance with real patients. Our earlier pilot randomized trial found very low engagement with a less structured LLM-based approach. Objective: This study aimed to assess the feasibility (adherence, acceptability, and data completeness) of a revised, structured LLM-based clinical reasoning laboratory (Laboratorio de Inteligencia Artificial [LIA]) in undergraduate physical therapy education and to explore its measurement properties, including its association with clinical judgment with a real patient assessed with the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR). Methods: In this single-arm pilot feasibility study, 27 third-year physical therapy students at a Spanish university completed, in 2024-2025, 3 virtual patient cases (lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine pain) simulated by ChatGPT (GPT-4) over 4 weeks, each twice. ChatGPT scored each attempt from 0 to 4 on the same 10 dimensions of the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR; 0-40 points) that human assessors applied (1-4 per dimension; 10-40 points) during a real patient encounter. Feasibility outcomes were case completion, data completeness, and satisfaction (0-10). Measurement outcomes were internal consistency and convergent validity (Spearman correlations between model-generated and human LCJR scores). Variability estimates informed the sample size of a future trial. Results: All 27 students were assessed with the LCJR; 22 (81%) completed at least 1 LIA case. Both attempts of the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic cases were completed by 78%, 63%, and 74% of students, respectively. Satisfaction data were available for 15 students (56%; mean 6.0, SD 1.3), and missing secondary data clustered in the third rotation. Internal consistency was excellent for the LCJR (alpha=.96) and ranged from .43 to .90 for model-generated ratings. Model-generated LIA scores clustered near the maximum (mean 36.0, SD 1.4). Among completers, LIA scores correlated weakly with the LCJR (rho=0.25, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.61; rho=0.44, 95% CI 0.05-0.71, when noncompleted attempts were scored as 0). Grade point average correlated almost perfectly with the LCJR (rho=0.96; n=22); after adjustment for it, the LIA-LCJR association disappeared (partial rho=-0.10). A future trial would require approximately 39 students per group (80% power, conservative variance). Conclusions: Delivering the LIA within the curriculum was feasible, but clinical judgment ratings generated by ChatGPT did not reflect those of human assessors with a real patient: they clustered near the maximum and showed no convergent validity once noncompletion was separated from performance. LLM-generated ratings should not be used as outcome or assessment measures without validation against human raters. Case calibration, completion tracking, and clarification of the GPA-LCJR relationship are also needed before a definitive trial. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06809634; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809634

items.title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
items.abstract_or_text: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator κ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

items.title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model
items.abstract_or_text: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin, and diagnostic delay is associated with complications. We tested whether longitudinal machine learning using electronic health record (EHR) data can identify incident IBD before diagnosis, and quantified lead time and deployment burden. METHODS: We studied adults with an IBD-compatible symptom, sign, or finding at UCSF (2012-2024). Incident cases were confirmed by structured filtering and validated large language model note review. We trained a state space model (Mamba) and comparators on pre-diagnostic EHR data, excluding diagnostic-workup features, and assessed discrimination at 6- and 12-month landmarks. We externally tested Mamba without recalibration at ZSFG, a safety-net hospital serving a demographically and socioeconomically distinct population, and simulated diagnosis-code-only deployment at UCSF. RESULTS: Six months after presentation, among patients still undiagnosed (67% of UCSF test cases), Mamba achieved an AUROC of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.928-0.999) at UCSF and 0.965 (0.952-0.976) at ZSFG. Median lead time was 20 months at UCSF and 15 months at ZSFG. Among future cases with an initially normal colonoscopy (N=32) or a histological finding of acute inflammation without chronicity (N=63), the model flagged 84% and 89% of these patients, respectively, before those procedures, indicating the potential for pre-diagnostic detection. Among 358,886 symptomatic patients not used for training (60 incident cases), the diagnosis-code-only model achieved an AUROC of 0.926; reviewing 20 alerts/month identified 34 cases (PPV, 1.09%; 64-fold above baseline). CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal machine learning can identify increased IBD risk months to years before diagnosis and may define a population for prospective studies of early IBD biology. Prospective evaluation should determine whether earlier identification reduces diagnostic delay.

items.title: Robust Detection of Directional Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks for Radiological Imaging
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning is now central to radiology, helping detect changes on X-rays, CTs, and MRIs. However, these systems are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks - small, crafted perturbations that mislead models while appearing unchanged to humans. Such errors risk missed cancers or false positives. Studies show over 90% attack success on medical scans. Almost 30% of US hospitals use AI in imaging in 2023. Thus, an effective method of detecting such attacks and their directionality is crucial to ensure the credibility and reliability of medical systems based on DNNs. We propose a novel detection framework that leverages subsequent attacks using random noise to identify adversarial perturbations. Our approach uses the analysis of variations in the Sigmoid function to distinguish genuine medical images from adversarially manipulated ones. Specifically, we compare prediction differences between clean and attacked images, as well as between different adversarially altered versions, to improve detection accuracy. We evaluated our method on three popular medical datasets including 'Chest X-Ray Images for Classification', 'Retinal Fundus Multi-disease Image Dataset' and 'Brain Tumor Dataset' under various attack scenarios, including random noise. Our framework achieved up to 99.8% ACC in identifying adversarial directional attacks, significantly outperforming existing defense mechanisms. It consistently identified adversarial samples across varying attack strengths while keeping false positives low, showing strong reliability and potential for clinical use. Furthermore, our proposal highlights its potential for real-world deployment.

items.title: Decoding super-enhancer regulatory grammar and pathogenic gain-of-function variants directly from DNA sequence
items.abstract_or_text: Super-enhancers (SEs) drive cell-identity gene expression, yet their identification relies on epigenomic profiling (e.g., H3K27ac ChIP-seq), precluding discovery in unprofiled cellular states and leaving their underlying sequence grammar unknown. Here, we present Borzoi-SE, a deep learning framework built upon the genomic transformer Borzoi that formulates SE discovery as hierarchical, cell-type-resolved genomic object detection directly from long-range sequence across 90 human lineages. Base-resolution attribution recovers lineage-defining master transcription factors across cell types. Within SEs shared across lineages, it reveals lineage-dependent motif usage, suggesting that the same regulatory regions can support distinct cell-type-specific programs. Using in silico ablation, Borzoi-SE decoded the functional hierarchy of the {beta}-globin super-enhancer, prioritizing hypersensitive site 2 (HS2) as the dominant constituent, which we experimentally verified via CRISPR interference. Trained without variant-effect labels, Borzoi-SE identified gain-of-super-enhancer variants in different tissues. At the CHRM2 locus, a single-nucleotide variant created a de novo glucocorticoid receptor (GR) motif that recruited activated GR and potentiated adjacent MEF2 regulatory syntax, nucleating a cardiac super-enhancer. Orthogonal multi-omics and population-genetic evidence linked this variant to increased CHRM2 expression and variation in resting heart rate and PR-interval duration. Borzoi-SE establishes a general framework for decoding SE regulatory grammar and prioritizing causal non-coding variants directly from sequence.

items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract_or_text: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

items.title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.

items.title: A Single-Cell Atlas of PVOD Across the Lifespan Reveals Cellular and Molecular Therapeutic Targets
items.abstract_or_text: Rationale Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD) is a progressive and lethal disease cured only lung transplant. While genetic mutations in EIF2AK4 have been identified in some cases, 70% of PVOD patients have no known etiology. Objectives To construct a single-cell atlas to define the cellular and molecular constituents driving pathophysiology in PVOD. Methods Lung samples were collected from four idiopathic non-EIF2AK4 mutation pediatric and adult PVOD patients and age-matched controls. Analyses of single-cell RNA sequencing, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and immunohistochemistry were performed to identify cell state changes and differential gene expression between controls and PVOD and subsequent transcriptome comparison between our PVOD and published pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) datasets. Measurement and Main Results The single-cell atlas reveals marked changes in the PVOD endothelium compared to controls. EndMT and ectopic COL15A1+ systemic venous shunts and pulmonary vein endothelium are hallmarks of PVOD. Molecular analyses reveal activation of the integrated stress response (ISR)/ATF4, TGF{beta} signaling, MAPK signaling, and BRD4 are potential key players in the pathophysiology of PVOD. While PVOD and PAH share both pathological and some molecular mechanisms, ISR and TGF{beta} signaling are more prominent in PVOD than PAH. Conclusions These data indicate that endothelial dysfunction is a primary etiology in the development of PVOD with activation of multiple pathways with druggable targets.

items.title: In Vivo Transcriptomics-Based Framework for Systematic Indication Expansion
items.abstract_or_text: Capturing the systemic effects of drugs in vivo remains a fundamental challenge for drug repurposing strategies. Here, we present an in vivo transcriptomics-based drug repurposing framework that profiles multi-organ RNA-seq from drug-treated rodents to model systemic drug responses and match tissue-specific drug signatures against a compendium of disease signatures for indication expansion. We applied this framework to semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist originally developed for diabetes and subsequently expanded for several other indications. By harmonizing more than 900 human disease transcriptomic signatures via agentic AI and using Z-transformed reversal of gene expression scoring to quantify drug-disease relationships, our approach successfully recovered established semaglutide indications while deprioritizing Alzheimers disease, an indication for which semaglutide was not effective. Top predictions for common diseases were supported by real-world electronic health record data from the Mount Sinai Health System and several predictions for rare indications are proposed for further investigation. This framework provides a scalable strategy for indication expansion across diverse therapeutic agents, especially investigational compounds for which real-world evidence remains sparse.

items.title: Cerebrospinal fluid dopa-decarboxylase is a biomarker of dopaminergic dysfunction
items.abstract_or_text: Background. Nigrostriatal dopaminergic dysfunction, a biological anchor of Parkinson's disease (PD), is routinely assessed using single-photon emission computed tomography of the dopamine transporter (DaT-SPECT). Dopa decarboxylase (DDC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a promising biomarker of dopaminergic dysfunction, but its association with DaT-SPECT has to be demonstrated. Objectives. To investigate the association of CSF DDC with DaT-SPECT. Methods. We first analysed proteomic and DaT-SPECT data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), including PD (n=891), prodromal PD (n=867) and healthy controls (n=161). We then verified this association in a single-center clinical cohort (UNIPG), including PD/Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) (n=78), atypical parkinsonisms (AP, n=11), other neurodegenerative diseases (OND, n=25) and controls (CTRL, n=40). Here, CSF DDC was measured by a novel fully automated quantitative immunoassay. Results. In PPMI, among 129 proteins assessed, DDC showed the strongest association with DaT-SPECT ({beta} = -0.132, FDR = 6.92 x 10-33). Across PPMI and UNIPG cohorts, DDC correlated with striatal binding ratio (SBR) ({rho} = -0.377, P < 0.001; {rho} = -0.466, P < 0.001, respectively) and accurately discriminated positive from negative scans (AUC 0.811, 95% CI 0.762-0.859; AUC 0.870, 95% CI 0.777-0.963, respectively). In PPMI prodromal cases, higher DDC predicted faster motor progression. In UNIPG, DDC distinguished PD/DLB and AP from OND and CTRL groups (AUC 0.830, 95% CI 0.764-0.896), independently of dopaminergic treatment. Conclusion. CSF DDC reflects nigrostriatal dopaminergic dysfunction, representing a potential quantitative biochemical alternative to DaT-SPECT that might be readily implemented via automated immunoassays.

items.title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
items.abstract_or_text: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC under a fixed training recipe. We find that these gains generalize across four additional evaluation settings, including the INSPIRE and eICU-CRD datasets, with improvements in macro AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 score. Our results show that simply changing how EHR data are presented to the model during pretraining can improve downstream performance, without changing the model or collecting additional data.

items.title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive, scalable source of quantitative biomarkers for the early diagnosis of brain disorders, and deep representation learning has become a powerful paradigm for extracting information-rich latent features from raw signals. However, neural networks tend to under-represent high-frequency information, a concern that is especially acute for EEG given its oscillatory nature and characteristic 1/f^χ power decay, which risks masking disease-relevant high-frequency signatures. In this study, we systematically investigate the spectral constraints of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoder architectures (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model. Using synthetic experiments and empirical validation, we show that while autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing, they remain biased against higher frequencies due to a magnitude-driven masking effect induced by the Mean Squared Error loss under 1/f-decaying spectra. Increasing latent dimensionality mitigates this attenuation but sacrifices latent compactness and generative stability. We argue that, as the field advances toward large-scale foundation-level feature extractors, it is imperative to move beyond simple time-domain reconstruction and to integrate spectral-domain loss terms and gradient-balancing techniques, so that the subtle high-frequency transients critical for diagnosing complex brain disorders are preserved in the latent representation.

items.title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.

items.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

items.title: Serum proteins predict incident inflammatory bowel disease 14 years before diagnosis: a machine-learning and Cox modelling in the UK Biobank
items.abstract_or_text: Using an analysis pipeline that combines machine learning-based feature selection with classical statistical modelling, we aimed to predict incident inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and to identify candidate proteins associated with disease development. We used UK Biobank data in an observational cohort study of 52,331 participants with proteomics data and without a history of IBD. The cohort was split into an 80/20 train/test dataset, and three separate extreme gradient boosting models were trained on the training dataset. Using Shapley values, we ranked the predictive importance of 2,912 proteins for incident IBD, Crohn's disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). The top 20 proteins per outcome served as features in multivariate Cox models predicting 350 incident cases over 14 years. All three proteomics Cox models showed moderate discrimination in the test dataset, with the UC model performing the best (C-index: 0.68), followed by IBD (C-index: 0.65), and CD (C-index: 0.60). All proteomics models outperformed clinical models. Smoking remained the only significant clinical predictor in the combined proteomics + clinical model. 48 unique proteins were identified across the three models, with 16 reaching statistical significance (p< 0.05). Machine learning-based feature selection with statistical survival modelling identifies plasma proteins that predict incident IBD and highlight biologically plausible, potentially targetable pathways in the preclinical phase of IBD.

items.title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental Design: This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. Results: Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression (p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression [≥] 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). Conclusions: MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification.

items.title: HybridDualPathNet: Cross-Fusion Attention of EfficientNetV2 and Swin Transformer for Brain MRI Classification of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Separating Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), and Healthy Controls (HC) using structural MRI remains challenging because disease signatures overlap and model performance can be strongly affected by data partitioning. We present HybridDualPathNet, a hybrid architecture combining EfficientNetV2-S for local features and Swin-Tiny for global context through a Cross-Fusion Attention (CFA) module. We evaluate the model in two experiments. First, on the Kaggle APD-3-Class dataset using an image-level split, the model achieves 98.25% accuracy. Second, on a combined Kaggle and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset containing 17,859 slices, we use a per-source split with patient-wise separation for ADNI subjects. In this setting, the model achieves 73.37% standard accuracy and a macro AUC of 0.880. Source-stratified evaluation reveals a substantial domain gap, with 91.2% accuracy on Kaggle test images and 59.2% on ADNI test images. Temperature scaling reduces expected calibration error from 0.130 to 0.015, while split-conformal prediction achieves 89.5% coverage. Saliency analyses using Grad-CAM++, Integrated Gradients, and occlusion indicate that model activations concentrate on brain tissue. These results highlight the importance of patient-level separation, cross-dataset evaluation, and uncertainty estimation when assessing MRI classification systems. The findings also show that strong performance on a single dataset does not necessarily translate to reliable generalization across imaging cohorts.

items.title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
items.abstract_or_text: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

items.title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

items.title: Cerebral microthrombi promote focal Cav-1-dependent blood-brain barrier impairment, triggering neuroinflammation and neuronal damage after traumatic brain injury
items.abstract_or_text: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is frequently accompanied by blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction, yet the microvascular events that initiate barrier failure and secondary neural injury remain poorly understood. Using highly sensitive fluorescent nanoscale tracers, correlative light and electron microscopy, single-cell transcriptomics, and genetic manipulation of Caveolin-1 (Cav-1), we show that BBB leakage after TBI in mice occurs focally at sites of cerebral microthrombus formation. Endothelial cells adjacent to microthrombi remain structurally intact, but exhibit a distinct transcriptional program enriched in both thrombosis- and transcytosis-related genes, including Cav-1. Microthrombi promote Cav-1-dependent transcytosis and size-selective extravasation of blood-borne proteins, exposing the surrounding parenchyma to circulating factors and inducing focal microglia activation and neuronal damage in vivo. In human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, these proteins directly impaired neuronal structure and network function. Genetic deletion of Cav-1 markedly reduces microthrombus-associated BBB leakage, immune-cell diapedesis, microglial activation and neuronal loss, whereas endothelial re-expression of Cav-1 using AAVs restores leakage. Human TBI data reveal early dynamic coagulation dysregulation associated with adverse clinical outcome, focal cerebral vascular injury and endothelial transcriptional signatures consistent with reduced barrier integrity and increased caveolae-associated transport. Together, these findings identify cerebral microthrombi as focal sites of Cav-1-dependent BBB dysfunction and establish pathological endothelial transcytosis as a mechanistic link between post-traumatic microvascular thrombosis, blood protein extravasation and secondary neuronal injury. Targeting Cav-1-dependent transcytosis may therefore provide a strategy to limit pathological BBB permeability and secondary injury after TBI.

items.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
items.abstract_or_text: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ^2-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

items.title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
items.abstract_or_text: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

items.title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
items.abstract_or_text: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links. Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)

items.title: EpiGuard: An Autonomous Infectious-Disease Early Warning Agent Platform
items.abstract_or_text: Infectious disease outbreaks often spread rapidly before signs of widespread transmission become apparent, leaving a big challenge for rapid response and effective intervention. However, current infectious-disease early-warning systems face three major challenges: fragmented epidemiological evidence across diverse surveillance sources, highly uneven data availability across diseases and geographic regions, and delayed warning procedure caused by manual data collection, analysis, and reporting. To address these challenges, we present EpiGuard, an autonomous, continually self-improving agentic platform for timely and reliable early warning of more than 50 infectious diseases across different regions. EpiGuard proactively monitors and captures newly released official surveillance records, using the latest available evidence for risk assessments. It dynamically adjusts its analytical strategy across three evidence availability regimes, enabling reliable risk assessment under diverse data conditions, ranging from the absence of historical observations to sparse and abundant evidence. Moreover, EpiGuard learns from the successful execution process by preserving effective data-acquisition and analytical procedures as reusable standard operating procedures, enabling it to progressively generalize to previously unseen diseases and regions. We use officially released infectious-disease surveillance data from the China CDC and the United States CDC to evaluate EpiGuard's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that EpiGuard outperforms state-of-the-art forecasting systems, improving forecasting performance by 9.68% and 14.04% on the China CDC and U.S. CDC datasets, respectively.

items.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Fusion Models to Predict Response to Venetoclax and Azacitidine in Patients with Newly Diagnosed Acute Myeloid Leukemia
items.abstract_or_text: Venetoclax and azacitidine (ven-aza) is a standard of care therapy for newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients unfit to receive intensive therapy, and may also be appropriate for certain fit patients. Models predicting response to ven-aza currently focus predominantly on genetics. Here, we present two multimodal fusion models: a custom ResNet-34-based model and a pathology foundation model fine-tuned for bone marrow smear (BMS) images that combine clinical and genetic variables with whole slide images. Training on 193 newly diagnosed AML patients who received ven-aza, we obtained an area-under-the-receiver-operating-characteristic (AUROC) of 0.79 and 0.82 for the ResNet-based and fine-tuned foundation models in a heldout test set, and 0.76 and 0.73 in an external validation set, predicting best response to this therapy. Sensitivity analysis showed that fusing image data with clinical and genetic variables outperformed training on either modality alone. In univariable and multivariable analyses, image-based classification was an independent predictive marker, second only in effect size to IDH1/2 mutation status, outperforming other genetic alterations. Image-based explainability showed high model attention on myeloblasts, suggesting previously unrecognized cell-specific patterns associated with response. Our findings suggest BMS images complement genetic biomarkers to refine outcome prediction in ven-aza treatment and incentivize AI-supported outcome prediction, including bone marrow morphology.

items.title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs
items.abstract_or_text: This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters. We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.

items.title: Cell Painting PLUS reveals phenotypic signatures for nephrotoxicity profiling in human RPTEC/TERT1
items.abstract_or_text: Multiplex high-throughput phenotypic profiling offers a cost-effective approach to monitor how chemical perturbations alter cellular morphology, thereby contributing to a mechanistic, human-centred hazard assessment with new approach methodologies in the context of Next Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA). In this study, we employed Cell Painting PLUS (CPP), an expanded high-content imaging assay that adds spatially resolved channels for mitochondria, lysosomes, actin, Golgi, RNA, DNA, and the endoplasmic reticulum, to renal RPTEC/TERT1 cells to evaluate nephrotoxicity. We profiled a set of nephrotoxic agents together with well-annotated reference chemicals encompassing diverse cellular targets to identify specific morphological profiles associated with distinct mechanisms of action (MoAs). Benchmark concentration modelling, correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering of RPTEC/TERT1 CPP data captured specific morphological signatures of more than 300 tested compounds and enabled discrimination between closely related and opposing phenotypes.
